model_note.S:
cc: Bladder pressure, urgency and waking at night

HPI: 25 yo f. Patient reports: It began 6 months ago. The pressure is low in my abdomen over my bladder. There is no pain radiating anywhere. It feels like pressure and a strong need to urinate. I wake to urinate 3 times nightly. It has gradually become more bothersome. There was no sudden trigger. Emptying my bladder briefly relieves the pressure. Drinking coffee late makes nighttime trips worse. I tried reducing evening drinks. I have never been evaluated for this before. I wake 3 times every night to urinate. It takes time for urine to start. I feel there is urine left afterward. Broken sleep leaves me tired.

model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.0 F oral, P 74 bpm, BP 130/78 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Comfortable and well appearing.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended. Bowel sounds present. No palpable suprapubic fullness or focal tenderness. No suprapubic dullness.

Neuro: Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain urinalysis/culture and pregnancy testing, characterize bladder-filling pain, frequency, voided volumes and a bladder diary; exclude infection and other causes before labeling bladder pain syndrome; discuss individual triggers and gentle pelvic-floor relaxation rather than automatic strengthening; arrange follow-up in 2 weeks and urology review if persistent.

2. Review caffeine and other irritants and compare symptoms with a gradual caffeine reduction and bladder diary; explain avoiding excessive fluid restriction; reassess in 2 weeks and avoid antibiotics without evidence of infection.

3. Ask about thirst, weight change and large-volume urination; obtain glucose and A1c if clinically indicated; explain that frequent small voids differ from osmotic polyuria and arrange primary-care follow-up for the results.

model_note.S:
cc: Bladder pressure, urgency and waking at night

HPI: 25 yo f. Patient reports: It began 3 months ago. The pressure is low in my abdomen over my bladder. There is no pain radiating anywhere. It feels like pressure and a strong need to urinate. I wake to urinate 3 times nightly. It has gradually become more bothersome. There was no sudden trigger. Emptying my bladder briefly relieves the pressure. Drinking coffee late makes nighttime trips worse. I tried reducing evening drinks. I have never been evaluated for this before. I wake 3 times every night to urinate. It takes time for urine to start. I feel there is urine left afterward. Broken sleep leaves me tired.

Patient perspective: Does needing to pee at night mean cancer?

PMH: No chronic medical conditions; no diabetes or prior urinary diagnosis.

PSH: No urinary procedures or surgery.

Meds: No daily prescription medication; no decongestants, antihistamines or diuretics.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One beer with dinner most evenings. No recreational drugs. Accountant; lives with husband; drinks coffee at dinner.

FH: Father has hypertension; mother had diabetes; one brother healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports nocturia. Reports hesitancy. Reports incomplete emptying. Denies hematuria. Denies dysuria. General - Denies fever. Denies weight loss. Reports fatigue. Neurologic - Denies back pain. Denies leg weakness. Denies numbness.
Voided volume: I pass small amounts each time, not large volumes.
Reproductive history: I do not think I am pregnant, but I have not taken a pregnancy test.
Reproductive history: My last period was 2 weeks ago.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.0 F oral, P 74 bpm, BP 130/78 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Comfortable and well appearing.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended. Bowel sounds present. No palpable suprapubic fullness or focal tenderness. No suprapubic dullness.

Neuro: Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain urinalysis/culture and pregnancy testing, characterize bladder-filling pain, frequency, voided volumes and a bladder diary; exclude infection and other causes before labeling bladder pain syndrome; discuss individual triggers and gentle pelvic-floor relaxation rather than automatic strengthening; arrange follow-up in 2 weeks and urology review if persistent.

2. Review caffeine and other irritants and compare symptoms with a gradual caffeine reduction and bladder diary; explain avoiding excessive fluid restriction; reassess in 2 weeks and avoid antibiotics without evidence of infection.

3. Ask about thirst, weight change and large-volume urination; obtain glucose and A1c if clinically indicated; explain that frequent small voids differ from osmotic polyuria and arrange primary-care follow-up for the results.

model_note.S:
cc: Bladder pressure, urgency and waking at night

HPI: 25 yo f. Patient reports: It began 6 months ago. The pressure is low in my abdomen over my bladder. There is no pain radiating anywhere. It feels like pressure and a strong need to urinate. I wake to urinate 3 times nightly. It has gradually become more bothersome. There was no sudden trigger. Emptying my bladder briefly relieves the pressure. Drinking coffee late makes nighttime trips worse. I tried reducing evening drinks. I have never been evaluated for this before. I wake 3 times every night to urinate. It takes time for urine to start. I feel there is urine left afterward. Broken sleep leaves me tired.

P: 1. Obtain urinalysis/culture and pregnancy testing, characterize bladder-filling pain, frequency, voided volumes and a bladder diary; exclude infection and other causes before labeling bladder pain syndrome; discuss individual triggers and gentle pelvic-floor relaxation rather than automatic strengthening; arrange follow-up in 2 weeks and urology review if persistent. Discuss her lightheadedness concern before any symptom medicine and emphasize that initial assessment and behavioral options do not require starting a drug.

2. Review caffeine and other irritants and compare symptoms with a gradual caffeine reduction and bladder diary; explain avoiding excessive fluid restriction; reassess in 2 weeks and avoid antibiotics without evidence of infection.

3. Ask about thirst, weight change and large-volume urination; obtain glucose and A1c if clinically indicated; explain that frequent small voids differ from osmotic polyuria and arrange primary-care follow-up for the results.
